description:
We are DMA, a software team from San Pedro Sula, Honduras, building real web systems. For Field Shift, we want to build a decision-support tool that helps Honduran farmers plan crop rotations using NASA Earth data. We're looking for developers with strong logic and problem-solving skills who adapt quickly to new tools, data and projects like Field Shift

. Beginners welcome. Bilingual team (Spanish/English).
summary:
Don Adrian's Farm, a smallholder maize and bean farmer in Catacamas, Olancho, Honduras, plants the same crops every year. The canícula (the July–August dry spell) is getting longer and less predictable, so they lose the first harvest while the soil degrades year after year.

Surco is a decision-support tool that shows the farmer the real climate of their area using NASA POWER data and builds a 12-month planting plan with the crops that best withstand it. The farmer picks their municipality on a satellite map, and the app explains why each crop is recommended and in which months to plant it. They can also watch their plot month by month in a simulation.

Surco does not replace the agricultural technician: it is a tool to explore options and arrive better prepared to talk with one.
details:
Surco: crop rotation planning for smallholder farmers in Honduras, powered by NASA data

What it does and how it works

Smallholder farmers in Honduras are planting into a climate that no longer follows the calendar. The mid-summer drought, the canícula, is getting longer and harder to predict across Central America’s Dry Corridor. Surco helps farmers decide what to plant and when, using NASA climate data for their own location.

The farmer picks a place by choosing a department and municipality, tapping the map, or using their device location. Surco pulls the climate history for that spot from NASA POWER (rainfall, evapotranspiration and maximum temperature) and classifies the area as rainy, dry or balanced. From there, the farmer can:

  • Explore the local climate: see month-by-month rainfall and which months are risky for planting.
  • Build a yearly plan: let Surco recommend the best rotation, or enter their current crops (1–4 of 22 supported crops) and see how they fit the local climate. The plan is shown by quarter or semester, and every period comes with advice and the reason behind it.

Benefits and intended impact

Most smallholders plant the same crops every year, even as rainfall patterns shift. When the first harvest fails, the season is lost and the soil degrades a little more. Surco turns 30 years of climate data (1996–2025) into a plan the farmer can bring to their agricultural technician. It does not replace expert advice. It gives the farmer and the technician a shared starting point. Over time, better rotations should mean fewer failed harvests, healthier soil and more resilience in vulnerable regions such as Lempira and Choluteca.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, and MapLibre for an interactive map with 3D terrain. Deployed on Vercel.
  • Backend: a Go API (https://github.com/DMA-Teams/nasa-app-api) that serves the climate history and runs the crop rotation engine.
  • NASA and open data:
    • NASA POWER (Agroclimatology community): daily precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), evapotranspiration (EVPTRNS) and maximum temperature (T2M_MAX)
    • NASA GIBS: Blue Marble satellite imagery
    • SRTM: elevation and 3D terrain
    • geoBoundaries: Honduras department boundaries
  • Reliability: API responses are cached and local backup data is bundled, so the app keeps working if the backend or NASA POWER is unavailable.

What makes it creative

  • Map first, no friction: the map is always visible and a side panel guides the user one step at a time. There are no forms, no jargon and no login.
  • Local language: we use words Honduran farmers already know, like canícula, instead of generic drought indices.
  • Data you can see: an illustrated field shows the crops through the year, and the sky changes with each month’s rainfall, so farmers can understand the data without reading a chart.
  • Explained recommendations: every period in the plan says why it is suggested, based on that location’s real climate.

Factors we considered

  • Users: many farmers have low digital literacy and use mobile phones with unstable connections. The interface is simple, mobile-friendly and works offline where possible.
  • Local accuracy: NASA POWER data comes in grid cells of roughly 50 km, so neighboring areas can share values. We state this openly.
  • Honesty: anything still simulated or estimated is labeled “(simulated)” in the app.
  • Expert review: Surco supports decisions rather than prescribing them. Final choices should be checked with local agronomists.
  • Open by design: NASA POWER needs no API keys, so anyone can run or fork the project.

GitHub repository: https://github.com/DMA-Teams/nasa-app
